This dataset lets us create a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct model with appealing cost-proof tradeoff compared with state-of-the-art commercial models like Claude Sonnet 4.5. It also significantly outperforms models like o4-mini and previously proposed research models. The training dataset produced by this work is available on HuggingFace.

TL;DR: VeruSyn scales verified Rust/Verus training data through self-synthesis, tutorial-based synthesis, and agent trajectories to reduce proof-synthesis costs.

Machine learning agents solve tasks through sequences of costly experiments, during which their knowledge needs evolve with observed results.
Static retrieval, which retrieves skills only once at the beginning of a task, cannot adapt to these changing needs. 
We study skill retrieval as a sequential decision problem conditioned on experimental progress.
Preliminary study on MLE-bench reveal that repeatedly retrieving from the latest experimental state may introduce irrelevant guidance, disrupt promising experiments, and consume resources without improving outcomes.
This observation motivates three design goals: retrieving the \textbf{right} skill to address the actual problem encountered in the current experiment; retrieving at the \textbf{right} time, only when the model’s own knowledge is insufficient to solve the current problem; and using the retrieved skill in the \textbf{right} way, correctly executing it in the current experimental context.
We propose an experiment-state-aware retrieval framework that maintains a structured record of attempted approaches, validation evidence, unresolved failures, and remaining resources. The framework triggers retrieval when this evidence identifies a concrete need, selects skills according to their applicability and feasibility within the remaining budget, and integrates them into targeted experiments with explicit evaluation criteria. Subsequent observations update the experimental state and inform future retrieval decisions. We outline a controlled evaluation on MLE-bench that compares static, naive dynamic, and selective state-aware retrieval under matched resource budgets, measuring final task performance, experimental efficiency, and skill adoption. This work investigates when adaptive access to procedural knowledge can improve long-horizon experimentation and when retrieval instead becomes a source of interference.

TL;DR: We study whether state-of-the-art language models know when to retrieve skills, what to retrieve, and how to apply them effectively during long-horizon machine learning experimentation.

A valid curvature upper bound need not justify either a robustness certificate or an intervention on an intrinsic predictor property. We demonstrate this distinction for a last-layer relative-flatness proxy used in both settings. First, empirical-risk stationarity does not eliminate pointwise first-order loss terms: at a finite global empirical-risk minimum, the retained certificate expression underestimates a loss increase by over $210\times$. We derive a globally valid, gauge-invariant feature-space repair. Second, common-row softmax shifts preserve predictions and the exact contraction while making the proxy unbounded. Even standard reference-class choices double it on average relative to the centered representation. For a single fixed-feature example with at least three classes, scalar retuning generically cannot align the induced probability updates. Row centering gives the orbit-minimized bound and restores value and full-model gradient invariance under this symmetry. Across 45 paired one-step tests on algorithmic and image models, amplified shifts separate raw-regularized predictors while quotient-regularized predictors remain aligned. Long-horizon CIFAR-10 experiments show substantial, reversible suppression of generalization, while evidence for selective delay after memorization is less consistent. Together, these results show that validity as a curvature upper bound does not by itself justify either inversion into a robustness certificate or differentiation into an intrinsic training intervention.

TL;DR: A valid relative-flatness bound can still fail downstream: inversion may yield an unsound robustness certificate, while differentiation may induce representation-dependent training updates. We characterize and repair both failures.

Mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models store many expert weights, making precision allocation important under a tight storage budget. Existing allocation criteria can reduce average reconstruction error while increasing error on individual calibration sources. To address this challenge, we propose ASRA, Anchored Source-Robust Allocation, which judges precision exchanges relative to a fixed sensitivity base. ASRA measures joint expert errors on each source, converts them into projection costs, and compares each precision choice with the same base. It weights the largest source-wise increase by task sensitivity and adds the change in a shared structural cost, then uses an additive upper bound to select a static precision map within the base's spending limits. With gradient scales and structural costs held fixed, our analysis bounds the corresponding population objective while accounting for approximation and calibration uncertainty. We evaluate ASRA on three large MoE models at three budget levels. Among the evaluated quantized methods, ASRA achieves the lowest perplexity and KL divergence and the highest token agreement at every budget on DeepSeek-V4-Flash. It also leads all three metrics at the two higher budgets on Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B. These results show that ASRA can better preserve reference behavior under tight storage budgets.

TL;DR: ASRA allocates mixed precision in MoE language models by minimizing a tractable upper bound on   worst-source cost increases from a fixed base under storage constraints.

Staged latent pipelines must choose between holding a pretrained encoder fixed and adapting it at a small learning rate. These are not the same intervention at two magnitudes: setting the encoder timescale to exactly zero removes the encoder stationarity condition and enlarges the invariant set of the block gradient flow, so the zero-rate and long-time limits fail to commute. Our main result makes the resulting difference \emph{signed}. In a solvable overparameterized linear VAE with a teacher, where superfluous latents couple to the data noise floor $\eta$, every generic positive-rate endpoint attains generalization error $J(\kappa)$ for a U-shaped profile minimized at $\eta$, while freezing an encoder trained at control $\kappa_0$ retains $J(\kappa_0)$ exactly. The gap $J(\kappa_0)-J(\kappa)$ is therefore sign-definite: freezing beats \emph{every} positive encoder rate precisely when Stage 1 was better matched to the noise floor than Stage 2, in four analytically characterized regimes. Three corollaries sharpen this. Freezing at a Stage-1 equilibrium is exactly conservative, so the cost of the intervention is fixed by Stage~1 alone; the departure clock carries a misspecification factor $1/(\tau|\kappa-\kappa_0|)$, so continued training at the Stage-1 control never departs; and one nongeneric coincidence survives on an unstable invariant manifold with logarithmic escape. A further gap is invisible to generalization error entirely: mid-transient freezing can preserve basis-invariant signal--nuisance leakage that continued training removes. A matched scalar VAE supplies the exact phase portrait behind these statements, numerical integration confirms the phase diagram and both clocks, and controlled nonlinear denoising experiments recover the predicted helps-versus-hurts organization, while MNIST diagnostics in the appendix show that the $O(1/\tau)$ departure clock survives amortized inference.

Across multi-turn conversations and agent interactions, accumulated history increases prompt length and KV-cache memory. Compressing prompts and KV caches independently overlooks their coupling and the effects of compression on later turns. Removing text changes subsequent inputs and the caches derived from them, while evicting cached states changes subsequent attention without shortening the prompt. We formulate joint compression as a sequential decision problem over persistent memory units that link visible text to its corresponding KV entries across heads. LACING uses stable anchors to maintain this correspondence across interactions. The policy jointly conditions each compression decision on the unit's textual features and evolving KV-cache state. For each unit, a single categorical policy chooses whether to retain it, remove its text and corresponding KV entries, or preserve its text while sparsifying corresponding KV entries across heads. We train the policy online from task-level rollout groups to minimize cumulative GPU cost subject to utility retention relative to a fixed full-cache reference. Separate cost and utility credit mechanisms assign rollout feedback to individual compression actions. We evaluate LACING on Terminal-Bench 2.1, which measures end-to-end task success under interactive execution.
On 89 tasks, LACING solves 11 versus 10 with matched full-cache at 9.6% lower reported analytical backbone cost.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved strong results in improving large language models (LLMs) on tasks with stationary, verifiable rewards, such as mathe-matical reasoning and code execution. There, the environment follows fixed rules and does not adapt strategically to the agent. Strategic dialogue differs in this respect: the environment is another agent that adapts to the policy, and success depends on the interaction between the two sides. Despite this interactive nature, current RL approaches typically train a target agent against a static counterpart or simulator. We show that this paradigm produces brittle policies: they exploit counterpart-specific regularities rather than learn strategies that generalize across counterparts, and their performance collapses under counterpart shift—
most sharply when they face a copy of themselves. We formalize this failure as the static-counterpart mismatch and quantify it directly in our experiments. To address it, we propose Isolated Bilateral Reinforcement Learning (IB-RL), in which the two roles co-evolve through joint rollouts while each role optimizes its own reward through fully independent advantages, action masks, and update paths. We evaluate frozen policies against fully independent held-out counterparts in both domains. On Vehicle TeleSales, IB-RL achieves 89.6% Success@1, compared to 84.6% for the best unilateral RL baseline. On Deal-or-No-Deal, it reaches 98.4% agreement against DeepSeek V4 Pro, compared to 86.4% for the best unilateral baseline, whose agreement collapses to 46.2% in self-play. These results indicate that jointly training both roles with strict per-agent isolation produces policies that generalize more effectively to unseen counterparts.

Model predictive control with a learned world model selects an action by comparing candidate action sequences using predicted returns. This comparison creates selection bias i.e. even when each candidate’s prediction error has zero mean, the largest predicted return is optimistic, and the bias grows with the number of candidates. We formulate the decision to replace a reference action with the first action of the selected sequence as a multiple hypothesis testing problem. Using held-out planning contexts, we calibrate a lower confidence bound on the selected action’s continuation advantage and replace the reference only when the bound is positive. Under an exchangeability assumption across planning contexts, the rule controls the marginal probability of a replacement whose true continuation value is lower than the reference. Experiments in controlled examples and continuous-control benchmarks, including visual world models, show that the correction maintains its target error rate as the candidate budget grows, unlike validation-tuned uncertainty heuristics. In settings where model error changes the selected action, calibration improves first-action continuation value and closed-loop return.

TL;DR: World-model planners overrate the best of many candidates. We calibrate a selection-aware margin on the chosen action's advantage and replace a reference policy only when it clears, improving closed-loop return at a declared error level.

Contextual bandit algorithms are often deployed in real-world environments where contextual variables may be partially observed or missing due to factors such as sensing noise, privacy or cost restrictions, or incomplete responses from users. Surprisingly, not many works in the bandit literature have considered this problem despite its practical relevance. This paper introduces a novel logistic contextual bandit algorithm designed for environments with binary reward and partially missing contextual variables. We consider a challenging and realistic setting where both the missing variables and the missing mechanism are correlated with the observed ones. We incorporate a new imputation framework into the GLOC algorithm of Jun et al. (2017), and prove that the proposed algorithm achieves a high-probability regret bound $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ where $T$ denotes the time horizon with respect to a well-defined oracle. The validity of our theoretical analysis is further corroborated through experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating robust performance under missingness.

Controlling deformation in generated videos remains challenging for slender
objects such as cables, hoses, and ribbons. Specifying an object's path does
not determine how its shape should respond to material properties, loads,
and constraints. The underlying challenge is to model the distributed dynamics
that govern bending and rotation along the object. We introduce CosseratGen,
a framework that combines learned slender body dynamics with pretrained
video generation. At its core, the Direct-Time Neural Cosserat Operator
(DT-NCO) learns from Cosserat rod simulations to predict centerlines and
material frames given initial states and prescribed physical conditions,
at requested times within the learned horizon. Material frames capture the
orientation of local cross sections, distinguishing anisotropic bending
responses that the initial centerline alone cannot determine. Projected
predictions guide a frozen video generator, allowing physical conditions
to control deformation while the scene prompt specifies appearance.
Experiments demonstrate improved centerline prediction on withheld mechanics
compositions and improved structural adherence in generated videos.
By combining learned dynamics with generative priors, CosseratGen enables
control over slender object deformation through explicit physical parameters.

TL;DR: Physics-Grounded Video Generation for Slender Deformable Objects

Knowledge-tracing models trained across many learners capture population-level patterns but may misfit individuals as their ability, learning state, or response behavior changes. Online personalization can correct such errors, yet lower average loss may conceal substantial harm to some learners at intermediate points in their histories.

We propose AdaStudent, an online personalization method that leaves the population model frozen and adds two lightweight Bayesian residual experts. The long-term expert retains past evidence, while the short-term expert emphasizes recent observations. The frozen model remains a third expert, and their predictions are combined according to past predictive performance. In ideal arithmetic, giving the frozen expert an initial weight of 0.99 bounds the mixture's cumulative log-loss excess over the frozen model by $-\log(0.99)\approx 0.01$ for every learner and every prefix. A separate adaptive conformal layer updates prediction sets from previously observed responses to address coverage drift under distribution shift.

On 1,923 EdNet test learners, AdaStudent reduces average log loss with no observed numerical violations of this budget. Without hyperparameter retuning, it also improves log loss on 2,450 external test learners from ASSISTments 2009 and 2015, again with no observed budget violations. Online Platt scaling achieves larger average gains but exceeds the same prefix budget for 38.1–61.5% of learners under order stress tests. Separate experiments with a two-expert residual configuration show improved prediction under controlled shifts, while adaptive conformal updating brings empirical coverage closer to its target than a fixed threshold. Thus AdaStudent offers an auditable trade-off between average gains and learner-prefix risk rather than a guarantee of improvement for every learner.

TL;DR: AdaStudent personalizes frozen knowledge-tracing models with a three-expert mixture that improves average log loss on EdNet and ASSISTments while bounding each learner's prefix excess loss in ideal arithmetic.

Latent diffusion models increasingly exploit semantic representations from vision foundation models to improve image generation.
Yet models that jointly generate these representations alongside VAE latents discard them at decoding time, reconstructing images from the latents alone.
We introduce semantic-aware decoding, which conditions the decoder on both representations while keeping the pretrained generator and latent space fixed.
We further show that useful semantics need not be jointly generated: semantics extracted from a reconstruction and fed back to the semantic-aware decoder already improve generation, suggesting that conventional decoders do not fully exploit the information available in the latents.
Building on this observation, we train a semantic projector that predicts semantics directly from the latents, extending semantic-aware decoding to models that generate only VAE latents without an additional reconstruction at inference.
Experiments on ImageNet demonstrate improved generation across SiT, REPA, REG, ReDi, and REGLUE, spanning different model scales and both conditional and unconditional settings.
Semantic conditioning reduces generation gFID by up to 16\% over a strong latents-only transformer baseline, while also improving reconstruction rFID.
Our findings show that semantic representations can improve image synthesis even after sampling is complete.

Surgical robot autonomy holds promise for improving clinical efficiency, but reliable task execution requires a comprehensive understanding of surgical scenes.Such understanding extends beyond identifying entities and interpreting spatial relations to reasoning about key surgical steps and assessing the safety of surgical actions. Scene graph is a natural solution. However, prior works have yet to fully leverage this representation to connect visual understanding with action reasoning while integrating medical knowledge priors with patient-specific observations.

To address these challenges, we introduce SSGraph-R1 that trains vision–language model trained with reinforcement to generate surgical scene graphs, supporting visual understanding, task reasoning and emphasizing task-relevant relations.Using laparoscopic cholecystectomy as a testbed, we curate SSGraph-Scenes, integrating data with scene-graph annotations of key entities and relations. We further introduce SSGraph-Bench, a six-task benchmark that jointly evaluates visual perception, task understanding, and safety reasoning to assess models as the cognitive core for surgical autonomy.

Historical context in long-horizon forecasting contains recent states, recurring patterns, and older segments with heterogeneous predictive relevance. Directly extending the input history couples the accessible history length with the backbone's input budget. We therefore formulate historical context consolidation as a separate design dimension and propose the Temporal Memory Consolidator (TMC), which maps an H-step multivariate history to B memory slots through three complementary forms of memory: recent memory via direct retention, periodic memory via cross-period phase averaging, and event memory via learned aggregation of earlier segments. The recent and periodic operators are parameter-free, while the event aggregator is trained jointly with the backbone. This decouples the accessible history length from the backbone input budget without architectural changes. With one fixed configuration and no backbone retuning, TMC improves the backbone in 118 of 128 comparisons across eight datasets, four backbones, and four horizons, with an average MSE reduction of 8.55%. Compared with recent long-history plug-ins, TMC is the only method that achieves consistent improvements across all eight datasets and all four backbones, with the largest average improvement for every backbone.

TL;DR: TMC reorganizes a long history into a fixed budget of recent, periodic, and event memory slots fed to an unchanged forecasting backbone, improving 118 of 128 comparisons with a single shared configuration.

Physical interaction data often span systems with different underlying dynamics: the same action from a similar observed configuration can produce different outcomes. A short observation history may therefore be insufficient to predict the consequences of an action. We propose MetaDyn-JEPA (MetaDyn), a support-conditioned joint-embedding world model that uses additional interactions from the same physical system to inform prediction. MetaDyn encodes directed action--response transitions and aggregates them into a reusable world code that conditions multi-step latent prediction without test-time weight updates. Treating transitions as the units of evidence allows MetaDyn to aggregate support from disconnected fragments without relying on fragment-level sequence summaries. Across PokeWorld and MuJoCo, same-world support improves prediction over no-support baselines, while replacing it with wrong-world support degrades performance. MetaDyn remains stable under evidence-preserving repartitioning without fragment augmentation, and generally benefits from increasing same-world support toward the training length. In multi-dynamics Push-T, same-world support improves latent and physical prediction, and MetaDyn achieves higher reach-and-hold success than LeWM and LeWM + AdaJEPA. Overall, these results show that world-specific interaction evidence can provide a useful conditioning signal for prediction across varying dynamics.

Reusing data to choose and evaluate a model or query can introduce selection bias and alter sampling fluctuations. We introduce \emph{posterior drift profiles}, which measure the largest Wasserstein displacement of a data law under log-likelihood perturbations of bounded sensitivity. A profile bound has two uses: its value supplies the selection-bias allowance in transferring sample accuracy to population accuracy, while its integral yields concentration around the fresh-data mean, including after stable selection. Both guarantees use the original law's profile, so the same calculation can serve different selection procedures and statistics. We prove exact tensorization for product laws under additive metrics, even when selection induces posterior dependence. Explicit calculations cover bounded queries, sampling without replacement, and unbounded Lipschitz queries under metric privacy. The nonlinear Gamma profile shows why the profile's shape matters: increasing likelihood sensitivity can enlarge both bias and fluctuation bounds. A one-sided extension also accommodates asymmetric, dataset-dependent sensitivity.

Inference-time interpretability methods are usually published one at a time, on the
model, benchmark and metric their authors chose. Each is credible on its own terms. None
tells you what will help on the model and benchmark you have. We ran eight methods in
one harness over five models, seven benchmarks and two temperatures. All 1,700+ runs
were scored under one set of controls. Benefits are real. Seven of 26 model-benchmark
cells at temperature 1 show accuracy uplift that survives paired testing with
false-discovery control. Benefits are sparse. On a pre-registered random draw of
combinations we had never run, composition helps in 15 of 79 resolved cases. Stacking
two accuracy methods lands below the better ingredient in 17 of 21 rows. A working
combination is then cheap to keep, adding a median 1.7\% runtime. The cost of
composition is the search, not the deployment. Benefits are easy to overstate. Wherever
a result looked strong, a selection step was doing part of the work. Picking the best
method per cell qualifies 13 of 26 cells at a 3\% gain threshold. A null in which every
method equals its baseline reproduces that count. A prior that ranked combinations well
in hindsight returned only 1.32$\times$ enrichment when tested prospectively. One method
looked like it badly damaged confidence estimates. Measured against a like-for-like
baseline, there was no effect. We release the corpus, prompt sets, harness and
controls.

TL;DR: Mostly not. About one pair in six is beneficial, and you have to search rather than predict.

Speech language models are primarily built upon fixed-rate tokenisation schemes in which continuous waveforms are discretised into uniformly sampled codec tokens. A conventional transformer then allocates the same amount of computation to each token regardless of whether the associated speech is dense with information or silent. As speech information density is uneven, fixed-rate tokenisation can waste computational resources on regions of sparse information. We introduce the Adaptive Temporal Speech Transformer (ATST), an autoregressive speech generation model trained on 1,500,496 utterances (5,891 hours) from the People's Speech dataset. It applies entropy-based adaptive patch modelling to speech tokens to better allocate these computational resources. This is achieved by internally merging low-entropy tokens into "patches" based on predictive entropy. This strategy results in short patches in high-uncertainty regions, such as phonetic transitions, and longer patches in predictable regions, such as silence and sustained vowels. These patches are then used in place of raw tokens, substantially reducing sequence length for the majority of the model.
Experiments comparing entropy-based, fixed-length, and phoneme-aligned patches at matched patch lengths show that entropy patching improves modelling performance over fixed-length baselines at the same average patch length, winning on various acoustic consistency and naturalness evaluations. Phoneme-aligned patches lead only on lexical discrimination tasks and cannot run causally at inference. Entropy patching reduces the number of positions processed by the global transformer and lowers estimated compute as patch length grows, although the current implementation is slower in measured generation throughput.
At two tokens per patch, entropy patching halves the patch sequence length and reduces compute by 37%, while matching or improving the unpatched token-level model on consistency, lexical, and naturalness evaluations. Additionally, experiments show that patch boundaries naturally correlate with linguistic structure. Predictive entropy is therefore an effective signal for distributing a speech model's computation.

Transcribing music into a human-readable score requires a coherent understanding of rhythm, harmony, melody, and form. Two obstacles limit this goal: annotated recordings are scarce, and accurate local predictions can still produce inconsistent musical sequences. We present SheetSage2, a unified music transcription framework that combines synthetic data, task-specific structured decoding, and autoregressive distillation. Automatically annotated MIDI, rendered into audio, provides scalable supervision across music understanding tasks. Task-specific structured decoders integrate complementary musical cues and their temporal dependencies to produce musically coherent scores. Autoregressive distillation further retains transcription accuracy without task-specific dynamic programming at inference. Across eight benchmark collections, a single SheetSage2-AR model exceeds the listed prior systems on 12 of 15 benchmark--metric pairs in our evaluation, substantially improving over SheetSage1 and surpassing task-specific models on several benchmarks. Model weights and inference code are publicly available.

Dynamic MRI reconstruction from undersampled measurements is a challenging inverse problem that requires preserving both spatial reconstruction quality and temporal consistency across the frames of the cine series. While recent learning-based approaches achieve strong performance, they heavily rely on large training, mostly fully sampled datasets, and may otherwise generalize poorly. In contrast, training-data-free methods such as deep image prior (DIP) adapt directly to individual scans but often fail to fully exploit temporal structure and are prone to overfitting. They have been particularly attractive for dynamic MRI due to limited large, public, high-quality datasets.
In this work, we propose a structured DIP framework for dynamic MRI reconstruction that explicitly models spatiotemporal correlations through a low-rank plus sparse (L+S) decomposition. 
Instead of directly reconstructing the cine image series, we parameterize the low-rank (background) and sparse (dynamic) components using untrained convolutional neural networks following the deep image prior paradigm. 
We further introduce an autoencoder-inspired input–output consistency regularization, in which the network outputs are used to update the inputs recursively.
This formulation combines the implicit regularization of DIP with the interpretability of classical L+S regularization. 
Under the stated conditions, we analyze the fixed-input eADMM iterations underlying the practical algorithm, establishing a corrected Lyapunov-based sufficient descent property, asymptotic regularity, and primal feasibility of cluster points. 
Across various acceleration factors, and two datasets, our numerical results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms classical reconstruction and existing supervised and unsupervised MRI reconstruction methods.

Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) is a fundamental tool for combinatorial optimization with extensive real-world applications. A central challenge is designing computationally efficient MILP formulations. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to automate the modeling process, from deriving formulations to strengthening them. Reliable automation requires robust methods for verifying that proposed formulations preserve the underlying optimization problem. However, existing approaches evaluate formulations numerically and fail to reason about general problem instances. We resolve this limitation by introducing a constructive definition of MILP reformulation that can be formalized in Lean and machine-checked. We develop `FLARE` (Formulation-Level Automated Reformulation Evaluation), a method that uses an LLM-based agent and the Lean proof assistant to verify proposed reformulations against a reference formulation. To evaluate our approach, we introduce FormulationBench, a challenging dataset of 20 problems and 109 formulations. `FLARE` outperforms existing methods, with **100%** accuracy on the NP-hard subset of FormulationBench. Furthermore, `FLARE` produces a machine-checkable certificate for every reformulation it accepts. For cases where formal guarantees are not necessary, we introduce `FLARE-NL`, a fast and cheap LLM proxy that matches `FLARE`'s accuracy but produces no certificate. These methods enable reliable verification in automated optimization modeling.

LLM judges are increasingly central to evaluating AI-generated code, tests, and formal specifications, yet their reliability is still checked in the least scalable way possible: fresh human ratings for every new judge, prompt, model, and threshold. We challenge this validation loop by asking whether human judgment can be amortized and \textbf{scaled} through falsifiable behavioral properties. We propose a property-certification protocol for LLM judges of Lean~4 theorem and specification quality, where each judge is scored by four automatically testable conditions: identity, bug monotonicity, specification monotonicity, and repeat/prompt stability. Our variance-aware trust index \(\mathrm{TI}_{\mathrm{var}}\) is one instantiation assessed against human ratings of these diagnostics. The contribution is the method for combining falsifiable properties into an auditable trust signal, rather than asserting that particular weightings discovered on \(n {=} 75\) human-labeled development pairs constitute a universally fixed evaluator constant.

  On eight judge configurations spanning frontier prompts, weaker baselines, edit-distance, and random controls, \(\mathrm{TI}_{\mathrm{var}}\) strongly predicts judge-level human alignment on that development suite, reporting validation-set Spearman correlations of \(0.833\) (avg labels), \(0.905\) (pass1), and \(0.738\) (pass2). Property-level analysis shows that monotonicity under removed specifications is the strongest single predictor of human agreement, followed by monotonicity under injected bugs, while identity and stability are weaker standalone signals. Applied to \textsc{VeriBench}, the protocol illustrates development-set human agreement for scalable evaluation settings involving AI-generated code, tests, theorems, and formal specifications, while explicitly not claiming deployed generalization guarantees.

TL;DR: We propose a property-certification protocol for LLM code judges, showing that a variance-aware Trust Index predicts human alignment and supports scalable evaluation of AI-generated Lean 4 specifications.

Enterprise workflows require reliable, repeatable execution of long action sequences
in uncertain environments. Existing AI agents often represent a workflow as written
instructions (e.g. SKILLs), which discard executable evidence, or as scripts that
require explicit selectors, waits, and recovery logic. Both of them can be brittle
under noisy agent context or uncertain web environments. We present Browser
Process Automation (BPA), which compiles recorded actions, semantic DOM trees,
and observed effects into persistent and executable Robotic Process Automation
(RPA) workflows. Agents can parameterize, compose, and replay these workflows
without reconstructing prior reasoning or retaining the original context. During
replay, Sequential Monte Carlo resolves ambiguous targets; readiness checks ensure
actions run in valid states, and completeness checks verify their effects. Compiled
dependencies validate composition and pass variables to downstream actions. We
evaluate BPA on our Enterprise Workflow Benchmark: 36 long-horizon tasks
that process 292 records on 22 deliberately difficult and uncertain sites. With
lightweight Gemini-3.7-Flash, BPA achieves 98.6% perfect-task and 99.8% record
success. When turning the context to SKILL or compacting the context, BPA
preserves success while reducing token costs by 68.7–79.5%. The results show
that execution traces enable reliable enterprise automation at very low cost.

TL;DR: BPA turns agent- or human-recorded browser traces into persistent, programmable, executable, and composable workflows for reliable, deterministic, repeatable enterprise workflow use cases. .

Two-stage pipeline parallelism provides a simple and practical way to distribute large-model training across distinct compute domains. Its initial partition, however, can become inefficient during execution as available workers change, inter-stage communication degrades, or memory pressure shifts between stages. A runtime system must then decide whether to retain the current pipeline or change its stage widths, layer boundary, communication path, or execution placement. Such changes are not free: checkpointing, state movement, restart, and warmup can offset the benefit of a better post-reconfiguration plan.

We present GatePipe, a runtime framework for adaptive two-stage pipeline-parallel training. GatePipe continuously combines stage-level compute history, worker availability, memory constraints, activation-transfer characteristics, and network conditions to construct feasible pipeline configurations. It evaluates each candidate together with the cost of reaching it and changes the running pipeline only when the expected remaining useful work improves. This allows compute imbalance, network variation, and repartitioning overhead to be handled within one decision process.

Experiments on a four-A100 testbed show that GatePipe completes all 168 phases in focused no-probe runs and achieves 1.120× the useful work of static execution. In an 11-event multi-tenant trace, it completes all 66 target phases and produces 3.610M useful tokens. The results show that effective two-stage pipeline adaptation must jointly consider compute balance, communication conditions, and the cost of changing the partition.

TL;DR: GatePipe adaptively reconfigures two-stage pipeline-parallel training by jointly considering compute imbalance, network conditions, memory constraints, and transition cost.

In subjective, open-ended scenarios, individuals and even whole communities may develop implicit notions of quality that are unarticulated. What lies behind these quality judgments? Past work has implicitly modeled these judgments by training reward models on datasets of human preferences, or constructing LLM-as-a-judge methods. Instead, in this work, we seek to explain the underlying factors that predict human quality judgments. We propose \textsc{Atomic Metrics}, an interpretable framework that constructs fine-grained explanatory criteria across a population of pairwise-preferences. This method first induces atomic criteria by contrasting preferred and dispreferred responses, refines them using preference feedback, and learns the relative importance of each criteria. We use \textsc{Atomic Metrics} to improve LLM judges, showing that the learned \textsc{Atomic Metrics} are highly correlated with human preferences across a range of tasks and demographic groups. We also show that these preferences can be highly contextual and distinct, depending on the task context, and the community whose preferences are being studied. We further demonstrate that \textsc{Atomic Metrics} can be used to improve the performance of models, by guiding their generations in aspects that humans have revealed are important to them. Finally, we demonstrate the potential benefits of \textsc{Atomic Metrics} for individual personalization, where it is possible to learn specific tastes of individuals from just a few examples. Thus, this study seeks to shed light on the latent factors that predict observed human preferences in subjective open-ended tasks, as well as improve the training, evaluation, and personalization of large language models.

Existing approaches to long-context reasoning use direct inference, retrieval, compression, or agentic processing to access and manage long inputs. Our controlled analyses suggest that locating and retaining relevant text can be insufficient for tasks requiring dependency tracking or global aggregation. We propose TopoMem, a training-free framework that compiles evidence topology—how supporting facts are distributed and related—together with the required composition rule and answer schema into an executable memory contract. A restricted state-execution fast path handles supported event sequences; other queries use a hybrid compiler that reconciles query semantics with observable context structure to select a typed reducer or model-backed reader. The operator library spans 13 evaluated execution routes, including set construction, dependency closure, global counting, numerical execution, and semantic synthesis. With a frozen Qwen3.5-9B backbone across five benchmarks, TopoMem matches or exceeds BM25, ReadAgent-P, and LLM×MapReduce-v1 in all completed benchmark-level comparisons. Relative to the best-performing of these evaluated baselines on each benchmark, it improves scores by 14.31 points on LongBench-v2, 21.02 task-balanced points on InfiniteBench, and 33.80 points on BABILong. Gains over direct inference (Direct-HT) persist on the full-context-fit subsets of LongBench-v2 and InfiniteBench, although Direct-HT remains 1.11 points stronger on RULER. Routing ablations on a controlled RULER subset favor joint semantic–structural selection over either signal alone. These findings support constructing long-context memory around query-dependent computation rather than text retention alone.

TL;DR: TopoMem combines query semantics and evidence structure to select executable memory operations and neural readers for long-context reasoning without training the backbone.

Unsupervised anomaly detectors often learn representations and reference distributions from unlabeled data assumed to be predominantly normal. Unknown contamination can distort both the learned geometry and the reference bank used for scoring, but removing suspected anomalies can itself discard useful normal structure. We study when reference purification helps and when it does not. We introduce CI-DCUAD, which combines representation learning with contamination-invariant reference selection (CI-RS). Preliminary unsupervised scores select observations for representation warmup and final reference construction, while main-stage training returns to the complete unlabeled dataset. We characterize effective contamination and show that selection reduces anomalous reference mass exactly when normal observations are retained more frequently than anomalies, $q_N>q_A$. Purification alone, however, does not guarantee better detection, which also requires preserving normal support and informative reference geometry.

A controlled separability--contamination study comprising 840 runs identifies distinct failure, success, and abstention regimes. Purification is not practically reliable at zero separation, is reliable in every valid nonempty positive-separation condition, and yields empty selections in two extreme conditions. Across five tabular benchmarks, CI-selected reference construction accounts for most of the favorable F1 change on CreditCard2013 and NSL-KDD, but produces unfavorable effects on the remaining datasets. Neither reference-only nor CI-Full significantly exceeds the matched baseline over the complete structural-ablation grid after Holm correction, although CI-Full significantly exceeds both incomplete CI variants. These results show that reference purification is a conditional mechanism, not a universal robustness strategy, and characterize the conditions under which it succeeds, fails, or should abstain.

TL;DR: CI-DCUAD improves anomaly detection by purifying contaminated reference sets when normal and anomalous representations are sufficiently separable.

We study decentralized online learning in task-based Fair Value Games (FVGs), where heterogeneous agents repeatedly select tasks and receive their marginal contributions to unknown, \emph{identity-dependent} coalition values. We introduce \texttt{OSD-FW}, a projection-free Frank--Wolfe method that uses one sample per update and adapts a known template for \emph{non-convex} objectives. Its new component is a \emph{sampled drift correction}. The centralized form of that correction needs the joint change in every agent's policy, which no individual agent holds, and earlier decentralized methods substitute a compact summary statistic that identity-dependent values do not admit. Ours is built instead from single actions that agents draw and announce for themselves, at a per-round query cost linear in the numbers of agents and tasks. Because the Frank--Wolfe gap equals total exploitability in these games, the resulting stationarity bounds are Nash-regret bounds, with $\mathcal{O}(T^{3/4})$ under unilateral-oracle feedback, $\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3})$ once the correction is added, and $\mathcal{O}(T^{5/6})$ under pure bandit feedback, the last slower than the best rate known for this class. Under a matched value-oracle budget, the drift-corrected variant ranks fourth on average Nash gap but attains the smallest final-iterate gap among the decentralized methods tested.

Token-level sparse attention mechanisms such as DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) rely on a lightweight indexer to score every prefix position and select the top-$k$ tokens for downstream attention.
While this design reduces the attention cost to $\mathcal{O}(Lk)$, the indexer itself retains $\mathcal{O}(L)$ per-query cost and becomes the dominant bottleneck at long contexts.
Existing accelerations operate along spatial axes: sharing indices across layers (IndexCache), hierarchical search-space pruning (HISA), and indexer-head routing (MISA), each treating consecutive decode steps independently.
We identify a complementary temporal axis: adjacent decode steps share over 90\% of top-$k$ selections at 4K context and maintain 95\% stability among high-scoring core tokens even at 32K.
Based on this observation, we propose TISA, which partitions prefix positions into $K$ groups and refreshes only one group per step in round-robin fashion, reusing cached scores for the rest.
TISA requires no retraining, no architectural modification, and no custom GPU kernel.
Experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 show that TISA maintains competitive LongBench quality, preserves full Needle-in-a-Haystack accuracy at $K{=}2,4,8$ across contexts up to 128K, and achieves $3.8{\times}$ to $7.3{\times}$ indexer kernel speedup on NVIDIA H20 GPUs.

Repeated interaction can allow adaptive AI systems to learn which interventions are effective for a particular user, without reconstructing a complete model of that user. We study when such personalized threat learning is possible under a trusted mediation architecture. Our central abstraction is decision-relevant user information: information matters only insofar as it distinguishes user models that require incompatible near-optimal threat policies. We formalize this notion through policy-regret geometry and derive two algorithm-independent information requirements: a decision rate--distortion converse for low expected regret and a Decision--Fano bound for reliable near-optimal policy selection. These results yield finite-horizon prevention guarantees whenever defended interaction releases insufficient decision-relevant information. When learning cannot be prevented, we introduce an architecture-dependent inference--exposure frontier that quantifies when acquiring sufficient user information necessarily produces detector-visible evidence, yielding a finite-horizon incompatibility between reliable personalized learning and remaining undetected. Finally, we compose learning, detection, residual intervention actionability, and closed-loop sensitivity to bound reference-relative autonomy loss. A worked neuroadaptive healthcare instantiation illustrates how information restriction, authorization, auditing, reactive protection, and recovery realize the framework. Overall, the analysis identifies decision complexity, information release, exposure, actionability, and dynamics as distinct bottlenecks for defending adaptive systems against personalized threats.

Image reconstruction with a pretrained flow prior must reconcile proposed image changes with incomplete or noisy measurements. For a nonlinear measurement operator or latent decoder, fitting one reconstruction does not explicitly control response variation along a proposed change. Our training-free solver, BARIC, evaluates measurements at two symmetrically displaced states along each prior proposal. It moves their center to fit the mean response while penalizing the response difference, with offsets fixed during correction. The penalty discourages opposing probe errors from canceling. We correct two coupled trajectories separately and average their decoded images. We establish fixed-block affine equivalence to pointwise correction in exact arithmetic, analyze local nonlinear departures, and bound the final measurement residual. Across eight inverse problems, BARIC attains the highest reported mean peak signal-to-noise ratio among the compared methods on five pixel-space tasks using CelebA-HQ and seven latent-space tasks using DIV2K, with 100 images per
dataset. Objective ablations on 50 images per setting further show higher mean PSNR than pointwise fitting.

TL;DR: BARIC performs training-free image reconstruction with pretrained flow models by fitting the mean measurement response of two symmetric, flow-guided probes and penalizing their response difference.

AI/ML models are useful for the prediction of materials' properties. Recently, there has been great progress in developing Neural Network models to predict the properties of solids, molecules, and crystals, avoiding expensive and time-consuming laboratory testing. This paper involves both Graph Neural Network (GNN) and Large Language Model (LLM)-based models to predict material magnetic ordering in four classes: Non-magnetic, Ferromagnetic, Antiferromagnetic, and Ferrimagnetic. Material crystal structure information is fed into a GNN and also converted to semantic text descriptions and tokenized as input to a LLM. The models are trained, validated, and tested on a dataset which is a combination of Materials Project dataset, Magndata dataset, and a set of uranium compounds with magnetic ordering determined in laboratory testing, with an 80/10/10 (training/validation/testing) data split. The study features two stage training process to train feature extraction and classification separately, which is necessary to handle class imbalance in the dataset due to limited availability of data for certain classes (AFM and FiM). In the first stage, the feature extraction is trained; in the second stage, the feature extraction is frozen and the classification head is trained for the final classification task. Based on the two stage training, the proposed LLM and ALIGNN-LLM multi-modal approaches can achieve an average 90% overall accuracy on the testing dataset across the four classes, and high (80% - 90%) per-class precision, recall and F1-macro scores.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in emotion recognition and sentiment classification, yet the internal neural mechanisms underlying these emotional competencies remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the existence and functional roles of emotional neural circuits within LLMs through a systematic neuron-level probing framework. First, we construct a controlled emotion-eliciting dataset to isolate context-agnostic emotional representations. We then identify emotion-selective neurons by analyzing their activation patterns across different emotional categories and network layers. To validate the causal roles of these neurons, we employ targeted ablation and enhancement interventions, demonstrating that modulating specific neuron groups significantly alters the model's emotion prediction performance. Furthermore, we map the distribution of emotional neurons across model depths and reveal how these local components integrate into coherent global circuits that drive emotional expression. Our findings provide the first systematic evidence of structured emotional neural circuits in LLMs, offering new insights into the interpretability of emotional intelligence in artificial systems and paving the way for fine-grained cognitive assessment of LLMs.

Machine learning engineering (MLE) agents must improve predictive quality while satisfying file, dependency, permission, and submission contracts. Fixed workflows make such rules explicit but restrict adaptation; free-form ReAct preserves adaptation but couples state interpretation, option construction, and selection in one Thought. We introduce Route (Rule-Grounded Orchestration Using Traceable Evidence), a test-time controller around an unchanged ReAct executor. Route separates the next execution into Perceive, Construct, and Select: Evidence Agent compiles a provenance-bearing state, Action Agent forms contract-compatible candidates from traceable gaps, and Budget Agent chooses an action or Stop using verified outcomes and the remaining tool/token budget. Three agents read a Verified Experience Bank. A single Writer appends every decision round; only checked executions contribute outcome-bearing, reusable Profile evidence. Route obtains 88.39±1.12% Any Medal on MLE-bench Lite and 89.17±0.12% AUC on KuaiRec. With backbone, executor, tools, workspace, tasks, and budget fixed, Route has the highest mean in all six backbone–dataset comparisons, exceeding the strongest alternative controller by 1.36%–3.69%. Component removals lower both primary metrics, and verified warm-start has the highest mean in all six transfer cells. Codes are available in https://anonymous.4open.science/status/213D.

TL;DR: ROUTE wraps an unchanged ReAct executor with rule-grounded Perceive–Construct–Select control and verified experience, improving contract-valid MLE delivery and end-to-end performance under fixed budgets.

Streaming visual geometry models with full-history key–value caches face growing memory and attention costs, and bounding the cache requires irreversible decisions about which observations remain accessible to future frames. Existing
memory policies address this with increasingly elaborate designs that combine
multiple importance scores with recency windows, anchor modules, or spatial
archives, leaving unclear which component actually determines retention quality. We find that the model’s accumulated attention is the decisive signal. With memory structure and capacity held fixed, ranking frames by accumulated attention nearly halves KITTI depth error relative to key-space coverage and outperforms uniform and recency selection on all three evaluated datasets. Building on
this observation, we revisit the heavy-hitter principle from language-model caches
and introduce $\textbf{Heavy-Hitter Frames (HHF)}$, a training-free, chunk-causal memory policy for StreamVGGT. HHF retains, independently for each global-attention layer and head, the complete frames with the highest decayed accumulated attention, protects the first frame, and requires no recency window, anchor module, or
spatial archive. The rule is grounded in a tight bound showing that, under bounded
value norms, the worst-case attention-output error of eviction within a chunk is
exactly proportional to the discarded attention mass, providing a local objective
for memory selection. Under the OVGGT evaluation protocol, HHF achieves the
best reported results in most evaluated settings across 3D reconstruction, camera
pose estimation, and video depth estimation, with efficiency comparable to prior
bounded-memory methods. On KITTI, with a smaller token budget than OVGGT,
it doubles throughput and reduces peak allocated memory by 27%. These results
indicate that, for bounded-memory streaming geometry, selecting memory by the
model’s own attention is more effective than elaborating the memory architecture.

Embodied intelligence requires agents to perceive, reason, and act in physical environments, thereby closing the gap between high-level semantic understanding and low-level motor control. Large Language Models (LLMs) provide strong commonsense reasoning, task decomposition, and semantic alignment, whereas Reinforcement Learning (RL) learns adaptive policies through environmental interaction. Existing LLM-RL systems for embodied agents remain limited by semantic-physical misalignment, weak transfer across environments and robot embodiments, and inefficient exploration in sparse-reward physical tasks. We present PhysLLM-RL, a hierarchical framework that couples LLM-based cognitive planning with RL-based policy learning through a physics-aware world model. The framework contains three components: a Physics-Infused LLM Planner (PILP) that injects physical priors through structured in-context reasoning, a Hierarchical RL controller that executes decomposed sub-goals, and Physics-Guided Reward Shaping (PGRS) that converts world-model predictions into dense, physics-aligned rewards. Experiments on BEHAVIOR, VirtualHome, and real robot platforms show that PhysLLM-RL improves task success by 17.8–32.4 percentage points across task categories, reaches 65.3% zero-shot generalization on unseen environments, and reduces exploration steps by 41.2%.

TL;DR: A hierarchical framework that injects physical priors into LLM planning and converts world-model predictions into dense rewards for RL, raising embodied task success by 17.8–32.4 points.

Frontier coding agents are bottlenecked not by their raw reasoning but by their tool repertoire: every new domain demands a hand-curated library of helper functions and harnesses that no current self-improvement pipeline learns to produce on its own. We introduce AgentForge, an agentic RL framework in which a Proposer and a Solver engage in asymmetric self-play to synthesize, validate, and version the agent's own tool library, with the self-play RL phase requiring no external task supply beyond a warm-start SFT stage. The Proposer drafts an executable task with a hidden test bundle; the Solver returns a candidate skill or a calibrated abstention; a deterministic four-stage gate (syntax, execution, novelty, abstention) decides whether the candidate is written to a persistent retrieval-indexed library. Both policies are co-trained with GRPO under a verifiable composite reward of pass-rate, novelty, and abstention. On three open code-agent suites, AgentForge lifts a Qwen3-8B base from 16.83%/10.21%/17.46% to 53.18%/34.71%/41.06% Pass@1 over five self-play iterations, beats a matched-compute ToolGen-RL baseline by 11.91/9.55/9.44 points, grows the library to 287 reusable skills (vs. 137), and cuts the hallucinated-tool rate from 24.60% to 2.58%; the library transfers zero-shot from competitive-programming proposals to ML-engineering tasks. Against the 2025--2026 frontier closed-weights agents (GPT-5.1, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok 4.20), our 14B model reaches an 86.2% score ratio of the strongest agent on BigCodeBench-Hard and closes 55.4% of the open-vs-closed gap; it further edges past Grok 4.20 there and, at 45% of its active parameters, surpasses the open Kimi K2 mixture-of-experts on ML-engineering transfer, with all code, adapters, and library snapshots to be released under Apache-2.0.

TL;DR: AgentForge uses asymmetric self-play between proposer and solver code agents to build a gated tool library, raising Pass@1 on three suites from 16.83/10.21/17.46% to 53.18/34.71/41.06% and cutting the hallucinated-tool rate to 2.58%.

Scientific-image representations often encode acquisition conditions together with the underlying physical or biological content, limiting robustness across microscopes, imaging settings, and laboratories. We ask whether matched observations of the same scientific content acquired under different conditions can directly reveal this nuisance variation in frozen representation spaces. We introduce Paired Acquisition Subspace Learning, a simple method that forms matched embedding differences, estimates their dominant directions with train-only singular value decomposition, and removes the resulting low-rank subspace without retraining the encoder. Pair-specific controls using pooled PCA, random subspaces, and shuffled correspondences test whether improvements arise from meaningful pairing rather than generic dimensionality reduction. Across metallographic benchmarks, the method suppresses acquisition information and improves paired alignment, while controlled negative results show that the assumption is not universal: learned nonlinear factorization does not reliably improve upon the analytic projection, and cross-magnification transfer fails a precommitted alignment criterion. On an independent specimen-disjoint cross-microscope benchmark, frozen configurations pass a one-time sealed test in all four ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50 conditions. Acquisition-leakage reduction ranges from 0.415 to 0.591, paired-distance reduction from 21.7% to 56.9%, and cross-domain retrieval and material-phase prediction improve in every condition. Specimen-cluster bootstrap intervals remain favorable for acquisition suppression and paired alignment in all four conditions. These results show that, when acquisition changes behave as a shared nuisance transformation, matched scientific observations can expose a compact removable subspace in frozen visual representations.

TL;DR: Matched scientific observations expose removable acquisition-associated subspaces in frozen visual representations, improving cross-acquisition alignment without retraining the encoder.

Exact global mass balance constrains one scalar property of a predicted field: its total mass. In an open system, sources and boundary exchanges change the required total mass from one step to the next. We develop a diagnostic framework to examine how specification of this total separates from spatial prediction error in finite-volume neural PDE surrogates. The results show that global mass balance must be assessed through both target specification and the field error that remains. A misspecified target can be satisfied to numerical precision. Even when the target is correct, the mass-changing error fraction varies widely across predictions, and fields satisfying this target can still differ substantially in spatial accuracy. Furthermore, omitting prescribed external mass increments can severely degrade autoregressive rollout stability. These distinctions appear across different mesh geometries and model constructions. Thus, a small absolute constraint residual only establishes agreement with the supplied target mass, without showing that the target was specified correctly or that the predicted field is accurate. Therefore, evaluating conservation-aware surrogates requires reporting how the supplied target mass is specified, the absolute constraint residual, spatial error, and rollout behavior together.

Unified multimodal encoders map inputs from different modalities into a shared representation space, but adversarial perturbations can destabilize modality-specific representations and disrupt the sample-level semantic neighborhoods required for zero-shot prediction and cross-modal retrieval. Methods that constrain an attacked tower through task alignment, pointwise feature consistency, or class-level calibration do not explicitly ensure semantic agreement across jointly adapted modality towers. We introduce \textbf{UniRob}, an adversarial fine-tuning framework for jointly robustifying the video, audio, depth, and infrared towers of LanguageBind. UniRob combines established adversarial contrastive and feature-consistency objectives with a new \emph{Distribution-Consistent Modality Alignment} (DCMA) objective. DCMA characterizes each feature by its similarity distribution over a batch of frozen text anchors. It aligns adversarial distributions with detached same-modality clean references and, when paired four-modality tuples are available, with clean distributions from paired counterparts across all six modality pairs and twelve directed alignment terms. We train on $11{,}773$ VIDAL tuples containing video, audio, text, and generated depth and infrared views, then evaluate zero-shot robustness on four primary modality-specific benchmarks. Compared with FARE, the strongest matched baseline, robust scores increase from $11.2$ to $14.2$ R@1 on MSR-VTT, from $14.5$ to $19.5$ Top-1 on ESC-50, from $45.5$ to $51.2$ Top-1 on NYUv2, and from $65.7$ to $72.0$ Top-1 on LLVIP under the primary modality-specific attacks. Component and graph-structure ablations show additional gains from DCMA beyond adversarial contrastive training and feature consistency. We also evaluate cross-modal retrieval on held-out VIDAL tuples with generated depth and infrared views and test sensitivity to stronger attacks. Our conclusions are limited to the digital, norm-constrained settings considered here. Code is available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/unirob-iclr2027-88F8/}.

Multi-robot systems, particularly heterogeneous robot swarms, can improve the efficiency of complex task execution through parallel collaboration and complementary capabilities. However, conventional rule-based methods rely on predefined task models and specialized decision making programs, making it difficult to understand complex semantic instructions and coordinate heterogeneous robots. LLMs introduce strong language understanding and task reasoning capabilities, allowing multi-robot systems to interpret instructions, decompose tasks, and assign roles according to task semantics. VLMs further incorporate visual perception, enabling robots to reason about objects, regions, and spatial relationships in physical environments. Nevertheless, existing LLM/VLM based methods often depend on known maps, centralized and synchronized decision making, limiting their generalization to heterogeneous robots and unseen tasks. We therefore propose a zero shot framework that combines decentralized asynchronous reasoning, lightweight information sharing, capability aware collaboration, and a unified action interface, enabling general purpose VLMs to generate robot specific actions executed by learning free experts without task or robot specific training. Experiments across diverse scenarios and multiple VLMs show success rates above 70%, with completion time reduced by up to 55.8% relative to the geometric greedy baseline.

Continuous language flows generate sequences in a smooth embedding space, yet their behavior under deployment shift remains largely unexplored. We introduce Domain-Aligned Embedded Language Flows (DA-ELF), an online target-label-free adaptation method for Embedded Language Flows. DA-ELF predicts before updating, combines stopped pseudo-labels with labeled source replay, and aligns rolling source and target populations through entropy-regularized optimal transport over full-sequence prototypes. The encoder, base flow, and vocabulary projection remain frozen, while only low-rank adapters, domain embeddings, and prototypes are updated. A matched control differs only in the two alignment weights, isolating alignment from ordinary self-training. Across question answering, summarization, translation, and unconditional generation, five-seed evaluations yield matched effects of 1.27 Natural Questions F1, 1.60 XSum ROUGE-L, 1.21 macro SacreBLEU, and 1.27--1.40 target Fréchet distance. All five prespecified paired comparisons remain significant after Holm correction. Ablations distinguish sequence-level prototype alignment from generic moment matching, while source probes and deployment measurements expose the corresponding retention and cost tradeoffs.

TL;DR: DA-ELF provides optimal-transport-coupled prototype alignment for target-domain adaptation in continuous language flows.

Autonomous post-training agents are ranked inconsistently at low compute. The PostTrainBench evaluation reports that its strongest agent scores 23.2 ± 1.8 against a few-shot base-model baseline of 18.1 and an instruction-tuned ceiling of 51.1, with per-benchmark standard deviations reaching ±50.8 on a benchmark whose mean is 30.8. Scaling compute resolves the ordering but only slowly: in the larger-compute PostTrainBench+ setting, the four-way ranking of frontier agents changes eleven times between 70 and 1,000 H100-hours, a cutoff drawn uniformly from that interval reproduces the 4,000-hour ranking 0% of the time, that ranking first appears near 1,284 hours, and most baselines plateau past 2,000 hours. We argue that a large share of this low-compute noise is not exploratory scientific search but wasted commitment. A trajectory analysis of 1,338 released runs finds that the training strategy is fixed before any code executes and then changed in only 2.1% of adjacent training pairs, that it tracks the agent rather than the task—one scaffold anchors on full SFT in 80.7% of runs, another on PEFT in 89.6%—and that it is plastic only within a short window before the first training run, after which neither accumulated experience, diagnostic advice, nor 7.9× the inference compute reopens it. The execution-level counterpart is equally visible: agents burn budget relearning public post-training knowledge—which trainer implements a recipe, which option combinations are supported, which datasets are decontaminated, which answer format an evaluator expects—and no baseline makes DPO work on ArenaHard even though length-normalised DPO and APO-zero are published operators. If the ceiling of a run is set by its initial strategy, the pre-execution window is the intervention point that matters. We therefore build a resource- and time-aware look-ahead Planner module that front-loads retrievable prior before any training GPU is used: a DeepResearch stage that retrieves target-relevant papers and candidate datasets, a seeded corpus of TRL documentation and TRL-cited method papers, and three planning agents—a data-recipe synthesiser, a training-recipe synthesiser, and a budget-aware combiner that fuses both reports into one executable recipe fitted to the wall-clock and GPU envelope. We integrate the module into a two-agent execution harness and evaluate on eight targets: the seven PostTrainBench benchmarks plus HealthBench-Hard, under a 12–14 h, four-H100 campaign. The planner-conditioned harness improves the weighted composite by +X.X points over a matched no-planner ablation and reaches its first above-base checkpoint ∆t GPU-hours sooner. HealthBench-Hard acts as a built-in control: because no public recipe targets it, the prior-quality hypothesis predicts the planner’s smallest advantage there, which is [confirmed/refuted] by our runs.

TL;DR: How to effectiely build autonous

We study hierarchical domain generalization as a problem of extrapolation from finite observed regions to an entire instance space, replacing i.i.d. sampling with arbitrary domain hierarchies. We show that the central obstruction is not only the complexity of the hypothesis class, but the train/test domain partition through which evidence is revealed. In particular, on an infinite domain, for any class with more than two hypotheses and any training size, some partition makes generalization fail for some target. These results suggest that modern generalization theory must treat domain structure as a first-class object.

Single-cell foundation models typically treat each gene as a token, which is both
costly and wasteful. A cell can express thousands of genes, so one token per gene
makes self-attention expensive, yet many of these genes are detected at low levels
and carry too little signal to deserve a token of their own. Genes that are expressed
together could instead share a token, leaving separate tokens for genes that stand
out. We introduce scTAT (Transcriptome-Aware Tokenization), which pairs a
gene-set vocabulary with a per-cell tokenizer. The vocabulary holds overlapping
gene sets that recur with stable relative expression across the pretraining corpus.
Using these sets raises two difficulties. First, which genes should share a token de-
pends on the cell, whereas existing multi-gene tokens fix the grouping in advance.
Second, gene sets of different sizes must be compared with single genes on a com-
mon scale. The tokenizer therefore decides per cell, letting gene sets and single
genes compete for token positions under an expression score normalized by the
square root of set size. Training still reconstructs individual genes, so predictions
stay at gene resolution. In frozen-embedding cell-type annotation, scTAT matches
the strongest one-gene-per-token model with half the token budget. Its advantage
over one-gene-per-token models at the same budget grows as the budget shrinks
and the tokenizer assigns more positions to gene sets. Encoding the same genes
with gene-set tokens also nearly halves the Transformer’s matrix-multiplication
cost. These results show that a token need not hold exactly one gene: when the
tokenizer decides per cell which genes share a token, a fixed budget covers more
of each transcriptome at no cost in annotation accuracy.

TL;DR: We’re running controlled ablations of Group-token selection, group size, token budget, and loss to determine when grouping improves single-cell representation learning.

Autoregressive video generation must preserve object states after interactions, occlusions, and viewpoint changes. Full-history Key--Value (KV) caches provide this context at growing cost, while bounded recency-based caches can discard relevant evidence. We introduce \textbf{Training-free Operation Delta Cache (TF-ODC)}, a fixed-budget memory that retains native historical KV at selected token positions. History-guided writer layers provide value features for motion-aligned novelty and persistence scoring. The selected indices are shared across layers, while each layer preserves its own keys and values in a Delta Bank alongside Sink and Recent Dynamics. Experiments on MemoBench and human and robot manipulation show that selective retention preserves strong object-identity and revisit scores while approaching Full-KV perceptual and motion quality. Paired qualitative comparisons examine revisited objects, manipulation outcomes, and uniform retention at the same historical-KV budget. TF-ODC requires no retraining and bounds historical KV growth independently of rollout length.

Although 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has achieved remarkable progress in photo-realistic novel view synthesis, the pure point-based representation lacks explicit geometric topology, restricting scene manipulation and deformation editing.
Recent mesh-based Gaussian methods alleviate this issue by binding Gaussians to mesh triangles, yet they inherently follow a geometry-first paradigm: Gaussian allocation and optimization are strictly constrained by mesh subdivision density. This leads to a fundamental perception-geometry mismatch: geometrically dense but visually flat regions waste representation capacity, while visually complex texture regions suffer from insufficient Gaussian modeling.
This paper aims to tackle the challenge of achieving manipulable photo-realistic rendering. We propose P-MGS, a Perceptual-aware and decoupled Mesh-Gaussian Splatting framework that addresses both representation allocation and geometric controllability.
First, P-MGS proposes a multi-view perceptual complexity guided Gaussian allocation strategy, which adaptively allocates Gaussian primitives according to surface appearance characteristics instead of mesh subdivision density, enabling more efficient utilization of Gaussian representation capacity.
Furthermore, we propose a decoupled optimization and manipulation paradigm, where Gaussian primitives are optimized independently from mesh structures and subsequently associated with meshes through post-hoc binding. This design restores the adaptive densification capability of vanilla 3DGS while preserving the original mesh topology, and further enables explicit geometric manipulation through the established Gaussian-mesh correspondence.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that our P-MGS achieves superior novel-view synthesis quality with more compact Gaussian primitives. More importantly, it retains flexible mesh-driven deformation and editing capabilities, effectively alleviating the inherent trade-off between rendering fidelity, representation efficiency and geometric controllability in existing mesh-Gaussian methods.

TL;DR: A Mesh Gaussian Splatting framework that allocates Gaussians by percplexity and enables mesh-driven manipulation without sacrificing 3DGS optimization flexibility.eptual com

Robust left ventricular segmentation in echocardiography remains challenging across patient populations and acquisition conditions. Large-scale vision--language pretraining provides transferable cardiac representations, but global image--text alignment does not directly establish pixel-level membership. We propose \method, a framework that adapts a frozen echocardiographic foundation model through supervised local semantic fields. Fixed text prototypes describe the left ventricular blood pool, background, imaging view, and cardiac states. Their spatial similarities to visual features drive layer-wise residual adaptation and segmentation decoding. Balanced semantic-field supervision directly trains the left-ventricle--background distinction while equalizing contributions across classes and spatial stages. A stage-wise refinement decoder aggregates same-resolution features before recovering spatial detail across scales, and the final classifier reuses the same foreground and background prototypes. This design provides a common discriminative reference for feature adaptation, intermediate supervision, and output prediction without updating pretrained encoder weights. Experiments on EchoNet-Dynamic, EchoNet-Pediatric, and CAMUS demonstrate that \method\ outperforms all competing methods in both in-domain and cross-domain segmentation without using target-domain data for adaptation or model selection. The anonymous project page is available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/w/echoclipseg/.

TL;DR: We adapt a frozen echocardiographic foundation model for generalizable left ventricular segmentation using supervised local semantic fields.

Privacy-preserved Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification (VI-ReID) aims to learn cross-modal pedestrian representations without sharing raw camera data. Under the Camera Independence (CI) protocol, camera-level data isolation is coupled with modality discrepancy, resulting in a challenging decentralized cross-modal learning problem. Existing approaches typically aggregate same-identity representations across clients into a unified global representation, overlooking the heterogeneity of cross-client identity relations under CI.
We observe that same-identity cross-client relations naturally consist of intra-modal and inter-modal relations, where inter-modal relations provide substantially greater benefits to VI-ReID. Moreover, inter-modal relations typically exhibit larger same-identity relation distances, providing an effective cue for discovering latent cross-modal relations without modality labels. Based on this observation, we propose Global-ID Relation Discovery to model client-level relation structures from shared-identity relation distances and uncover latent client groups. We further introduce Cross-Group Identity Discrimination (CGID) to exploit the discovered structure for identity discrimination in remote identity spaces, together with Hard Identity Relation Alignment (HIRA) to strengthen challenging same-identity cross-client relations. Extensive experiments on three VI-ReID datasets under CI protocol demonstrate the effectiveness of explicitly distinguishing and modeling heterogeneous cross-client identity relations, yielding substantial improvements in privacy-preserved VI-ReID.

TL;DR: We uncover and exploit heterogeneous cross-client identity relations under Camera Independence to improve privacy-preserved VI-ReID without relying on modality labels during training.

Evaluating relational visual reasoning requires more than a single aggregate accuracy: models may differ across relation types, task formats, and output requirements.
