We introduce StructCAPTCHA, a diagnostic benchmark built from visual reasoning CAPTCHAs, covering twelve mechanisms across physical consistency, topology and connectivity, spatial relations, and counting. Four linked evaluation views assess individual candidate judgments, exact-set selection over six-candidate grids, controlled relational variations, and question-polarity consistency. The evaluation separately records semantic correctness, output-protocol compliance, and infrastructure failures. Across 58,200 responses from six vision-language models under a single-request protocol, individual-candidate accuracy ranges from 42.0% to 65.2%, whereas exact-set accuracy ranges from 1.6% to 24.3%. Source-linked comparisons show that this task-level gap does not imply a uniform decline in cell-level accuracy within grids, highlighting the need to distinguish local judgments from complete-set correctness. Performance is strongly mechanism-dependent: the strongest model on the full benchmark achieves 84.4% exact-set accuracy on region relations but only 0.4–2.0% on physical-consistency tasks. An exploratory human study with 462 main trials yields 39.2% exact-set accuracy, compared with 25.8% for the same model on matched items, indicating that these tasks also remain challenging for humans. Together, these findings motivate evaluating relational visual reasoning across mechanisms and granularities, while accounting for output compliance. StructCAPTCHA provides a controlled testbed for characterizing these distinctions in multimodal model evaluation.

TL;DR: StructCAPTCHA diagnoses relational visual reasoning in vision-language models across twelve mechanisms, distinguishing individual-candidate accuracy from complete-set correctness.

We investigate whether cyclically varying the class composition of training batches can modify both the performance and the internal organization of neural networks. Motivated by nonequilibrium systems, in which cycling between related sub-goals can make switching between their solutions increasingly efficient, we introduce Dynamical Batching (DB), a sampling protocol that periodically emphasizes each class while leaving the loss and the optimizer unchanged, and compare it with Uniform Batching (UB), in which every mini-batch has equal class proportions. In the regime where standard training fails, DB changes the outcome: on a three-arm spiral, a capacity-limited MLP that plateaus far below perfect accuracy under UB fits the training data under DB. Tracking individual weights, we find that under DB the change between class-specialized states is carried by a smaller set of weights than under UB, and that this set is markedly more persistent from cycle to cycle, on every synthetic dataset we test and in a wider network that fits the data under both protocols. This organization is a signature of the protocol rather than a predictor of its benefit: it appears equally where DB leaves accuracy unchanged. In a channel-narrowed ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, the same protocol yields modest generalization improvements. These results show that how class emphasis is distributed in time can shape both the solution a network reaches and the internal structure of the network.

TL;DR: Cyclically emphasizing different classes during training rescues capacity-limited networks and concentrates class switching onto a small, persistent set of weights.

Existing federated person re-identification (ReID) methods mainly adopt parallel aggregation, enabling collaborative training without sharing raw data. However, this paradigm requires periodic synchronization and server-side aggregation, while aggregating heterogeneous client updates may weaken client-specific identity-discriminative knowledge. To address these limitations, we introduce the sequential federated learning paradigm into ReID, termed Sequential Federated ReID (SeqFedReID), where a single model is passed across clients and updated in sequence. This paradigm avoids periodic global aggregation and progressively acquires domain-specific identity-discriminative knowledge through client-wise updates, improving the utilization of heterogeneous knowledge. Nevertheless, cross-client domain discrepancies and disrupted historical feature relations can cause severe catastrophic forgetting. Hence, we propose SeqFedPAR, a Prompt-Affinity Relation Preservation framework for SeqFedReID. Specifically, we introduce a Shared-Domain Prompt Memory (SDPM) into a ViT-based ReID model, where S-Prompt is designed to encode client-shared identity-discriminative knowledge, while D-Prompt provides an expert memory for client-specific domain patterns that support identity discrimination. Based on the prompt memory, we further propose Prompt-Guided Relation Distillation (PGRD), which leverages sample affinities to the historical D-Prompt memory to estimate the relevance of pairwise relations to learned domains, and selectively preserves critical feature structures. Extensive experiments on four ReID benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves source-domain retention and target-domain generalization under sequential federated training. The code will be publicly released.

TL;DR: We propose SeqFedPAR, a prompt-based sequential federated ReID framework that decouples shared and domain-specific knowledge and preserves historical feature relations to mitigate cross-client knowledge interference and catastrophic forgetting.

Physiological data record the continuous evolution of human states over time, yet turning these recordings into reusable analytical capabilities still relies heavily on customized pipelines tailored to specific devices, modalities, and tasks. Large language models can understand analytical objectives, while domain-specific operators can perform specialized computations. However, complex tasks still require a common interface between the two that preserves measurement semantics and enables tasks, programs, and results to be shared and understood. We present PhysioHarness, a unified task and execution framework for healthcare research. Task instructions, tool observations, and repair traces are further organized into reusable training resources. It connects heterogeneous physiological signals with computational capabilities through task contracts. Typed programs are organized using PhysioIR to compose domain-specific operators in a structured manner. The execution of complex physiological tasks is further supported by contract-aware routing, quality and temporal constraint propagation, feedback-driven repair, and evidence binding. Experiments show that, compared with six advanced agents and frameworks, PhysioHarness improves the overall score across four capability categories by 9.4%–47.9%, while reducing the error risk from 12.6% to 2.8% at the same coverage level. Our results demonstrate that progress in physiological intelligence depends not only on model capabilities, but also on how domain knowledge is organized into shareable, executable, and learnable resources. PhysioHarness provides a unified research interface for the continual collaboration of physiological data, domain algorithms, and large language models.

Cauchy activations provide an analytic trial space for solving linear
partial differential equations by direct least squares. We develop
Cauchy Feature Collocation (CFC), which fixes complex poles outside the physical domain
and recovers output coefficients from PDE, boundary, and initial
constraints. Closed-form mixed derivatives assemble the operator
matrices, and a singular-value decomposition determines the
coefficients without gradient descent. For targets holomorphic on a
neighborhood containing the pole contours, we prove geometric
approximation of a fixed finite jet with shared coefficients.
Output-specific identities describe recovery from the fitted constraints.
Controlled heat and plate experiments show that direct Cauchy fitting
achieves lower field and differential errors than coefficient-only Adam
under identical matrices and objectives at the tested optimization budget.
Comparisons with fixed tanh, sine, Gaussian RBF, and Chebyshev dictionaries
using a common direct solver reveal a problem-dependent ordering:
Cauchy attains the lowest heat differential error, while sine features
lead on plate accuracy. In a separate study of sparse values and slopes
across analytic near-singularity families, Cauchy-Complex obtains the
lowest aggregate error for held-out higher derivatives.

Spatial interference and temporal confounding interact when treatments affect neighboring units, change their future states, and influence subsequent treatment decisions. Estimating causal effects therefore requires understanding how treatment effects propagate across locations and accumulate over time. We propose a network-based neural g-computation framework for estimating node-level effects of network-wide treatment sequences from observational data. Our central idea is to evaluate each treatment sequence through the evolving local and neighborhood states it induces. The framework jointly models spatial dependencies and temporal state dynamics, combining residual state modeling with stochastic trajectory averaging to estimate expected potential outcomes under alternative treatment sequences. This formulation captures how treatment effects travel through spatial connections and persist through changing states. We establish causal identifiability under explicit assumptions and derive a finite-sample generalization bound that quantifies how mechanism-learning errors propagate through coupled spatial and temporal dependencies. Experiments across synthetic grids, semi-synthetic social networks, and a real COVID-19 case study demonstrate the effectiveness of TrajGC across diverse spatial-temporal intervention settings. The results show that modeling extended treatment–state histories and integrating over stochastic state trajectories are important for accurate causal estimation, with increasing trajectory samples substantially reducing treatment-effect error. On the COVID-19 data, TrajGC reduces 7-/14-day treatment-conditioned outcome reconstruction RMSE by 39.2%/33.1% relative to the strongest deep baseline, further demonstrating its applicability to real networked systems.

Visual artifacts such as charts, technical diagrams, webpages, and document pages underpin scientific, commercial, and engineering workflows.
Editing these artifacts requires direct modification, dependency-aware updates, preservation of unaffected content, and compliance with domain constraints.
We define this capability as Visual Artifact Operation (VAO).
Prior benchmarks test parts of this problem, including cascading updates in charts.
We study direct edits, dependent updates, and preservation across visual domains and pixel, code, and agent paradigms under one image-only protocol.
We introduce Visual Artifact Operation Bench (VAO-Bench), comprising 1,573 manually screened tasks across nine artifact categories and three difficulty levels.
VAO-Bench uses executable artifacts and deterministic rendering to trace reference transformations and annotate direct edits, dependent updates, and preservation constraints.
All systems receive the same source image and instruction; we evaluate pixel-space editors, code-generating multimodal systems, and tool-using agents on direct-edit accuracy, dependency-aware update, content preservation, domain validity, and visual quality.
Experiments show that executable-code systems better support dependent updates, while pixel-space editors offer faster execution and strong visual quality.
Explicitly stating dependencies improves both paradigms, identifying implicit-update inference as a central bottleneck.
VAO-Bench provides a reproducible foundation for dependable visual artifact editing across generation paradigms.

Diffusion Bridge Models (DBMs) provide a mathematically principled framework for Image-to-Image (I2I) translation, but the need for many sampling steps limits practical application. While Consistency Models can accelerate sampling, adapting them to bridges (e.g., discrete CBMs) demands costly training and complex optimization. We propose Accelerated Bridge Consistency (ABC), a framework that distills pretrained DBMs into efficient few-step samplers without the heavy training overhead of prior methods. By formulating a Continuous-Time Consistency objective, we adapt continuous-time flow map distillation directly to bridge models. Combined with a proposed modernized network architecture, ABC achieves high-fidelity generation with minimal fine-tuning; reaching FID of 1.76 on DIODE (new SOTA) using only 2 NFEs - the first continuous-time I2I consistency solution.

TL;DR: In this work, we adapt continuous-time endpoint-map distillation directly for Diffusion Bridge Models, enabling fast Image-to-Image Translation.

Humanoid control, leveraging human demonstrations, has achieved diverse, agile, and natural locomotion behaviors through reinforcement learning (RL). While this paradigm has yielded remarkable performance in physical humanoid control, how to eliminate specific motions from learned policies remains insufficiently explored. Addressing this issue is motivated by pressing safety and privacy concerns: the removal of malicious, poisoned, or suboptimal motions, as well as copyright-protected motions subject to the right to be forgotten under regulations such as the GDPR, is of critical importance. To this end, we propose {ForgetMimic}, the first motion-level unlearning method designed specifically for physical-world humanoid control. The core idea of ForgetMimic is as follows: given a policy $\pi_\theta$ trained on $N$ motions, our method degrades performance on a target subset of $K$ motions while preserving the effectiveness of the remaining $N-K$ motions. Furthermore, we identify and resolve two key training mechanisms in robot control that lead to unlearning failure. We conduct extensive experiments on the Unitree G1 and H2 humanoid robots across 12 motions, including Dance, Fight, Flip, and others. Experimental results demonstrate that ForgetMimic effectively eliminates memory of designated motions while maintaining the normal operation of all other motions.

TL;DR: An unlearning method for reinforcement learning in humanoid control.

A continuously operating system accumulates observations, states, and past actions over time. 
Making use of this history requires more than retrieving information that appears relevant: a historical variable may be predictive of a decision while never participating in the process that produces it. 
Most memory systems for LLM agents organize past interactions externally and retrieve them based on similarity or recency, but these criteria do not reveal which parts of history a decision actually depends on. In this work, we formulate memory as a temporal dependency structure over execution trajectories. 
Rather than selecting historical records based on relevance alone, we recover variable--lag dependencies that describe which past variables participate in later decisions. 
Under standard identification assumptions for temporal causal discovery, the recovered structure can be estimated from repeated executions and used in two directions: selecting the historical records needed for future decisions and tracing past decisions back to the historical sources they relied on. Experiments in controlled environments and LLM-agent deployments show that the recovered structure identifies decision-relevant history while excluding predictive but unused variables. 
It enables selective memory retrieval with substantially reduced history and supports source-level attribution for auditing decisions under long and conflicting histories.

TL;DR: We recover the temporal causal structure behind an LLM agent's decisions from its logs, and use it to give each decision only the records it depends on and to trace which sources past decisions actually used.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves language-model reasoning through feedback on generated solutions. Experience replay can make this process more efficient, but its benefit depends on which experiences are retained and how they are replayed. To guide these decisions, we formulate online RLVR as a retrieval and ranking problem, with prompts as queries, responses as candidates, and verifiers providing relevance labels. This perspective yields a concrete selection principle: prioritize correct responses the model underranks and incorrect responses it overranks. Drawing on hard-negative mining in retrieval, we introduce \textbf{frontier replay}, which retains the lowest-ranked positives and highest-ranked negatives in bounded memory. We establish conditions under which frontier replay provably accelerates ranking convergence. Experiments show improvements
on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and demonstrate transfer to Amazon ESCI relevance classification.

TL;DR: We formulate online RLVR as retrieval, combining ranking-aware replay of weak positives and hard negatives with adaptive exploration to discover additional correct responses.

Simplicial neural networks (SNNs) are powerful tools for prediction tasks on
higher-order relational datasets stored on simplicial complexes (SCs), a higher-
order generalization of graphs. However, SNNs usually lack rigorous uncertainty
quantification (UQ), limiting their usefulness in high-stakes scenarios. We propose
conformalized SNN (CF-SNN), a framework that, given a simplicial-complex entity
with m prediction targets, generates prediction sets for all m targets simultaneously.
Under mild assumptions, CF-SNN guarantees that, for each target, the prediction
set contains the true label with a user-specified nominal coverage probability, and
the realized miscoverage proportion across all m targets is guaranteed to remain
close to the nominal level with high probability. Extensive experiments across
a wide range of SC prediction tasks demonstrate that CF-SNN is a flexible UQ
framework that achieves user-specified coverage while producing informative
prediction sets of small size.

Visual token pruning is an effective way to reduce the inference cost of VLMs, yet identifying a compact and sufficient subset of visual tokens remains challenging, as token importance depends not only on cross-modal relevance but also on complex, heterogeneous **Where--What** relations in each modality. Existing methods either prematurely mix position and content information into a shared representation or model them in separate stages, potentially obscuring their distinct structures and intrinsic dependency-relations. To address this, we introduce **Position-Content Dual Manifold (PCDM)**, a unified multimodal, multi-attribute relational system for visual token pruning. PCDM factorizes each token into coupled position and content nodes, thus forming two complementary manifolds per modality: a position manifold preserving native structural proximity and a content manifold capturing semantic correlations, with one-to-one node correspondence linking them together. The vision and language PCDMs are further connected through semantic alignment, enabling information to propagate globally across modalities and attributes while preserving their distinct structures. This enables inference of  higher-order task relevance and structured pairwise affinities among visual tokens. Token selection is then formulated as a budget-constrained quadratic optimization that rewards task relevance while suppressing semantic/spatial redundancy. Experiments across *five VLMs and ten benchmarks* demonstrate consistently superior efficiency--accuracy trade-offs over state-of-the-art methods. On LLaVA-NeXT-7B, PCDM retains 94.5\% of full performance with only 160 visual tokens (5.6\%).

TL;DR: A new relational system for jointly modelling multi-modal, where-what dependency among tokens

Language models now write much of the training data that other models learn from, and they are also asked to judge whether those labels are right. We separate three measurements that are usually run together: how much an annotation differs from a reference, how much of that difference a judge detects, and how much the annotation changes a model trained on it. We measure them on named entity recognition, receipt parsing and web action prediction in 305 training runs, under a pre-registered core protocol with documented exploratory extensions. On CORD, category confusions cost 9.8 F1 points at 50% corruption against 0.8 for content edits, yet every judge's detection rate under the default prompt is lower for the former. A frontier annotator disagrees with the CORD reference on 61% of receipts, but a student trained on its labels matches one trained on the reference, and a manual check of 200 differences attributes most of them to legitimate variants and reference problems. Synthetic edits matched to each annotator's footprint overestimate the damage of the strong annotator and underestimate that of the weak one. Fixed budget filtering by a judge improves training on both annotators' labels; random deletion of the same size and a reference labelled version of the kept receipts separate a selection part from a label source part that depends on which receipts were kept. Disagreement counts, detector scores and training outcomes should be reported together, none standing in for the others.

When a tool agent improves after training, how much of the gain comes from its learned policy, and how much comes from the interface through which it acts? We study this question by crossing training and evaluation interfaces that either require explicit answers or allow references to observed tool results. The study covers on-policy distillation, self-adaptation, reward-based training, and feedback-based training, with supervised controls, REST-derived tasks, database tasks, and 4B and 8B models. Changing the training interface has different effects under different evaluation interfaces: for 4B on-policy distillation, the same comparison yields -1.74 or +3.48 percentage points on 115 scored REST-derived tasks. Shorter outputs also need not improve accuracy: nine of ten fixed-weight interface comparisons reduce generated tokens, while four improve, three tie, and three decline. A separate intervention on 175 saved final-turn prefixes produces 101 additional submitted answers but only one additional correct answer, with 4.52 times as many final-turn output tokens. These results show why training gains, interface effects, answer submission, and computational cost need separate measurements when assessing progress in tool agents.

Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is challenging because severe illumination degradation makes visual information difficult to recover from the input alone. To address this issue, we propose VL-YUV, a vision-language-guided framework that incorporates high-level semantic priors into luminance-chrominance restoration. Specifically, SemFuse introduces illumination-related semantic guidance from a vision-language model, while Illumi and ColorRefine adaptively enhance luminance and refine chrominance, respectively. By combining semantic guidance with luminance-chrominance modeling, VL-YUV provides complementary information for low-light restoration. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, and ablation studies verify the complementary contributions of the three modules. Cross-dataset evaluation further shows that VL-YUV maintains competitive restoration quality without target-domain retraining.
